analysis.one_liner: Phases out nonessential uses of 'forever chemicals' and bans their release into the environment within ten years.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on this bill to phase out 'forever chemicals'; it died in the Environment and Public Works Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS, often called 'forever chemicals' because they never break down, are used in carpets, food packaging, cosmetics, clothing, and many industrial processes, and they have contaminated drinking water around the country. This bill would require makers and users of PFAS to report their use, submit phaseout plans, and stop all nonessential PFAS uses within ten years. It would ban PFAS in products like carpets, food packaging, cosmetics, and most apparel on faster timelines of one to five years, and make it illegal for manufacturers to release any detectable amount of PFAS into the environment after ten years. It would also let citizens sue violators and strip federal agencies of immunity from state PFAS rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drinks water, eats food, or buys consumer products: fewer PFAS in food packaging, carpets, cosmetics, and clothing means less exposure to chemicals linked to health harms, and fewer releases means less contamination of drinking water. People living near PFAS-impacted sites would get mandatory public notice and community meetings when endangerment is found.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone exposed to PFAS through water or products

how_it_helps.text: Beginning one year after enactment, the bill bans selling carpets, rugs, fabric treatments, food packaging, juvenile products, and oil and gas products that contain PFAS, with bans on cosmetics, indoor furnishings, apparel, and accessories following at two to five years.

Beginning ten years after enactment, all nonessential PFAS uses would be prohibited unless the EPA designates a use as essential, and it would be unlawful to release any detectable amount of PFAS into the environment.
Citizens could sue manufacturers or users violating the bill's requirements, and courts could award attorney and expert witness fees to prevailing parties.

Federal agencies would be stripped of immunity and made subject to the same federal, state, and local PFAS rules as anyone else, including civil penalties, with only a narrow, publicly reported presidential exemption.

The bill would establish Centers of Excellence for PFAS water testing and remediation research and create a state policy that PFAS contamination be cleaned up to levels that do not present an unreasonable risk.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and the many industries that use PFAS in products, from textiles and carpet makers to cosmetics and food packaging companies, would bear compliance, reporting, reformulation, and fee costs, some of which would likely be passed to consumers. Public water systems, treatment works, and waste facilities are explicitly excluded from the definitions of manufacturer and user.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers and PFAS-using product industries

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is heavy: every manufacturer and user must file reports and phaseout plans, and the default supplemental report fee is set at $100,000 if the EPA misses its own two-year deadline to finalize fees, though the agency may reduce fees for small manufacturers.

The ten-year deadline to phase out all nonessential uses and stop all detectable releases is aggressive, and some uses such as in medical devices, aerospace, or electronics may lack safer alternatives, forcing industries into the slow essential-use petition process.
Reformulation costs for products like rainwear and food packaging would likely be passed through to consumers, and some safer alternatives may perform worse than PFAS-treated versions.

Some observers of chemical regulation argue that a use-by-use petition process, with the burden on petitioners and fees per use requested, could let contested designations drag on well past the deadlines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside is large and broad: PFAS contamination of drinking water is one of the most widespread chemical pollution problems in the country, and the bill attacks it at the source. The costs fall on identifiable industries and eventually on prices, and the bill does include escape valves (essential-use petitions, research exemptions, a presidential exemption for federal agencies) that soften the burden but could also be used to slow the phaseout. On balance the trade favors ordinary people, though the timelines are ambitious enough that full compliance would be genuinely difficult.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, no one else signed on, the committee never acted on it, and the session of Congress ended before anything happened.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on April 18, 2024, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works; that was the only action it ever received.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill sat in committee with no markup, no report, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and the industries that use the chemicals in products, who avoided new reporting, phaseout, and release restrictions; the general public gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS makers and users; the public gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Forever Chemical Regulation and Accountability Act of 2024 in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup, reported it out, or advanced it to the floor.

against.name: Sen. Thomas Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 118th Congress, never brought the bill before the committee for action.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Democrat, ever supported the bill and no roll-call votes ever occurred, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would phase out nonessential production within ten years, require costly annual reporting with fees, and make any detectable release into the environment unlawful, with civil and criminal penalties. Their continued low-cost use of PFAS comes at the public's expense in drinking water and body burden contamination.

industries.industry: PFAS-using product industries (textiles, carpet, furniture, cosmetics, food packaging)
industries.note: Bans on selling PFAS-treated carpets, food packaging, cosmetics, furnishings, and apparel would begin one to five years after enactment, forcing reformulation. The health risk these chemicals pose to consumers is precisely why the products would be banned.

industries.industry: Public water systems and waste and treatment facilities
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes public water systems, treatment works, and waste management facilities from the definitions of manufacturer and user, sparing them the reporting fees and liability that fall on chemical makers even though they passively receive PFAS.

industries.industry: Environmental remediation and scientific research institutions
industries.note: The bill would fund Centers of Excellence for PFAS water testing and remediation research and allow manufacturers to transfer PFAS stocks to accredited research consortia, creating work and funding for these entities.

industries.industry: Defense, aerospace, and medical device manufacturers
industries.note: Uses critical to health, safety, or society can be designated essential through a petition process, so these industries could keep needed PFAS but only after proving no safer alternative exists and paying per-use petition fees.
